text.en: Meena saw a picture of Mohenjo-daro's great bath. "Cities this old?" she wondered.

Several early urban societies developed near major rivers, including the Nile, Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus system and the Huang He. Each region had distinct local conditions. Rivers gave fertile land and water for farming and travel.
Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are examples of Harappan cities with planned features. Mohenjo-daro is the site of the structure called the Great Bath. The Egyptians built pyramids and wrote in hieroglyphics, while Mesopotamians used cuneiform writing and the Chinese developed silk and the calendar.
In these societies, evidence points to exchange, specialised work, visual culture and organised institutions. Surviving signs and scripts differ in how much scholars can read. They left behind monuments and artefacts that tell us how people lived.

text.en: Archaeologists describe many ancient cities as centres that brought people, goods and institutions together. A city’s layout and objects can offer clues to how that arrangement worked.

board.text: Cities connect people, resources and institutions

text.en: A river can support farming by supplying water and depositing sediment. It can also offer a travel route. Flood timing and water management differ between rivers.

board.text: Rivers offered benefits and posed challenges

text.en: In Egypt, settlements concentrated along the Nile and its delta. Seasonal flooding could renew cultivated land. Nearby dry regions made the river corridor especially important.

board.text: Egypt: Nile valley and delta

text.en: The Egyptian king was known as the pharaoh. Monumental building required resources and organised labour. A monument shows that people could coordinate work on a large scale.

board.text: Monuments are evidence of organised work

text.en: The pyramids at Giza were royal tombs. The surrounding remains help researchers study the work needed to build them and the practices connected with burial.

board.text: Giza: royal tombs and evidence of labour

text.en: Egyptian hieroglyphs used written signs that could represent sounds and ideas. Writing survives on stone and also on materials such as papyrus, made from a plant.

board.text: Egyptian evidence: stone inscriptions and papyrus

text.en: The Rosetta Stone carried related text in three scripts. Scholars used the comparison to help read Egyptian writing. A known script can help test interpretations of unfamiliar signs.

board.text: Parallel texts can help decipher writing

text.en: Mesopotamia is often translated as land between rivers. The Tigris and Euphrates crossed a region with many cities and kingdoms over time. A region and a single government are different ideas.

board.text: Mesopotamia: many political centres over time

text.en: In parts of southern Mesopotamia, irrigation channels helped carry water to fields. This required work to build and maintain channels. The need for water shaped some collective decisions.

board.text: Irrigation links fields, rivers and labour

text.en: Cities such as Ur and Uruk became centres of work, trade and worship. A stepped structure called a ziggurat was associated with a temple complex.

board.text: Ur and Uruk · ziggurats

text.en: Cuneiform uses wedge-shaped marks. Clay tablets can record quantities, transactions and stories. Compare what a receipt and a story each reveal about their writers.

board.text: Clay tablets preserve different types of information

text.en: Hammurabi is associated with a collection of laws carved on a monument. A written law is evidence of a rule or ideal. It does not prove that every person followed it.

board.text: Law text shows stated rules

text.en: The Epic of Gilgamesh survives in Mesopotamian written traditions. A story can show what people imagined or valued. Historical claims about specific events need other kinds of evidence as well.

board.text: A literary source answers different questions

text.en: Early Chinese settlements developed in varied regions. The Huang He and Yangtze were important river systems, and the crops and farming practices of different areas were not identical.

board.text: Early China had more than one river setting

text.en: The Shang period left bronze objects and written inscriptions on bones and shells. Some inscriptions record questions consulted through divination. Archaeologists use them to study the Shang world.

board.text: Shang evidence: bronze objects and oracle bones

text.en: Look at a bronze vessel as both an object and evidence. Its material and shape can tell us about casting skills and use. Its find location adds context.

board.text: Object + find location support an interpretation

text.en: The Harappan civilisation covered many settlements. Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira and Lothal give different examples of how communities organised buildings, craft and water.

board.text: Harappan civilisation included many settlements

text.en: Street patterns, wells and drains suggest careful planning at a number of Harappan sites. Dholavira’s reservoirs show another response to water needs. Avoid assuming every settlement used the same design.

board.text: Different sites show different water systems

text.en: The Great Bath was found at Mohenjo-daro. Its construction shows careful management of water. Its precise purpose remains open to interpretation.

board.text: Great Bath: known construction, debated purpose

text.en: Harappan craftspeople made beads, seals and other objects. Weights and objects found across regions can support questions about production and exchange.

board.text: Manufacture and exchange leave material clues

text.en: Harappan seals often carry short sign sequences. The signs remain undeciphered, so we can compare their shapes and uses without claiming to know their complete meaning.

board.text: Indus signs remain undeciphered

text.en: Objects and historical references point to contact between the Harappan region and Mesopotamia. Exchange does not require the societies to have identical cities or beliefs.

board.text: Contacts link societies with distinct practices

text.en: Harappan cities changed over time, and smaller settlements continued after the major urban period. Scholars weigh several possible causes for change across regions.

board.text: Urban change varied across time and place

text.en: Pick two societies and compare the same kind of evidence. For example, compare tablets with seals, or large buildings with water structures. Name what each example supports and what it leaves uncertain.

board.text: Compare the same question across different evidence

problem.en: Compare what a Mesopotamian cuneiform tablet and an inscribed Harappan seal can tell us.

text.en: Identify what can be read in the script on the tablet.

why.en: A readable text may record a transaction, story or another specific activity.

text.en: Look at the Harappan seal’s signs and find context.

why.en: Its context and shape are evidence even though scholars have not deciphered the sign system.

prompt.en: A friend says Harappan cities had no planning. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: They had grid streets and drains.

points.en: Several early cities grew near major rivers, with distinct local conditions.
